title: Liberation without a single government
paragraphs: Japan’s surrender in August 1945 ended colonial rule, but it did not immediately create an independent Korean government exercising authority throughout the peninsula. Occupation arrangements developed under wartime and postwar decisions by outside powers. The 38th parallel became an administrative dividing line for the arrival and operation of Soviet and American forces, with consequences much greater than its original appearance on a map.

To understand the moment, imagine the difference between liberation as a popular celebration and liberation as an administrative problem. Korean activists, local organizations, returning exiles, foreign armies, and established institutions did not share a single plan for political authority. These overlapping claims made the months after the war unusually uncertain.
